candidateRows: Objective moral facts are moral truths whose validity does not depend on observers' attitudes, beliefs, or feelings.
This defines the central realist thesis and identifies the anti-realist alternatives that Huemer's opening argument seeks to eliminate.
At the outset of his opening statement, Huemer defines objectivity as attitude independence and frames realism through the rejection of three alternatives.
Error theory is implausible because at least some moral judgments, such as prohibitions on gratuitous cruelty, are exceptionally obvious truths.
Rejecting the claim that all moral statements are false is the first major step in Huemer's elimination argument for objective moral facts.
Huemer uses an extreme case of gratuitous suffering to argue that at least one moral proposition is plainly true, thereby rejecting global error theory.
The wrongness of gratuitous cruelty does not vary with individual approval, belief, sentiment, or social convention, so it is attitude independent.
This rejects stance-dependent accounts, establishing the attitude-independence component required for Huemer's conclusion that moral truths are objective.
Huemer tests several possible observer attitudes toward cruelty and argues that none changes its moral status, thereby rejecting subjectivist dependence.
Moral sentences function propositionally in embedded linguistic contexts, creating a serious problem for non-cognitivist accounts of moral discourse.
This eliminates the remaining major alternative in Huemer's argument and completes his route from ordinary moral discourse to objective moral facts.
Huemer explains non-cognitivism, develops an embedding objection using conditional and propositional constructions, and concludes that moral statements can be objectively true.
Radically skeptical denials of an entire philosophical subject matter are more plausibly products of philosophical bias than corrections of common sense.
The argument supplies a general diagnosis of anti-realist skepticism and supports Huemer's reliance on apparently obvious moral judgments as starting points.
Huemer compares moral skepticism with sweeping skeptical positions in other fields and argues that recurrent revisionism indicates a philosophical cognitive bias.
Moral realism is not a common-sense position because ordinary people need not possess determinate realist or anti-realist commitments at all.
This directly challenges the common-sense foundation of Huemer's realism and introduces Bush's central alternative of folk metaethical indeterminacy.
Huemer's claim that moral anti-realism is radically skeptical, revisionary, and contrary to common sense.
Bush rejects the characterization of anti-realism as revisionary and argues that ordinary moral practice does not require attributing either metaethical position to speakers.
Empirical studies do not clearly establish folk realism because methodological improvements reveal variable responses and widespread misunderstanding of metaethical questions.
The empirical and methodological critique undercuts Huemer's appeal to realism as the natural or prevalent common-sense interpretation of moral judgment.
Huemer's reliance on allegedly obvious and common-sense realist intuitions to support objective moral facts.
Bush surveys experimental work, emphasizes measurement and interpretation problems, and argues that non-philosophers often answer normative or epistemic questions instead.
Realist seemings can at most provide private initial justification and cannot settle the dispute for people who lack those seemings or require public corroboration.
This challenges the epistemic force of Huemer's intuitive elimination argument by denying shared seemings and distinguishing private warrant from public justification.
Huemer's use of intuitive appearances in his elimination cases as justification for rejecting anti-realist alternatives.
Bush grants that appearances may initially justify a believer, uses an analogy about uncorroborated experience, and denies that realist intuitions are shared or dialectically decisive.
Anti-realist quietism escapes the standard trilemma because moral language has context-sensitive, empirically determined uses rather than one uniform semantic analysis.
This presents Bush's principal positive alternative, denying that error theory, subjectivism, and non-cognitivism exhaust the possible forms of anti-realism.
Huemer's process-of-elimination argument that error theory, subjectivism, and non-cognitivism exhaust the alternatives to realism.
Bush rejects uniform semantic assumptions, proposes contextual and intrapersonal variation in moral speech, and concludes that folk discourse is often metaethically indeterminate.
Error theory appears counterintuitive only when pragmatic implications about an agent's attitudes are conflated with its narrowly metaethical denial of stance-independent facts.
This directly answers the realist appeal to apparently absurd consequences by explaining the appearance of absurdity through normative and pragmatic entanglement.
Huemer's claim that error theory has radically counterintuitive implications for ordinary moral judgments.
Bush distinguishes an error theorist's metaphysical commitment from the attitudes and conduct ordinarily inferred when someone denies a familiar moral statement.
Appraiser relativism does not entail endorsing another person's conduct, because the relevant moral assertion can instead report that person's approval.
The move rebuts another major branch of the realist argument that anti-realist semantics generate unacceptable conclusions about plainly objectionable conduct.
Huemer's objection that subjectivist theories make objectionable conduct morally acceptable whenever an agent approves of it.
Bush argues that the relativized truth of an approval report is trivial and carries no requirement that the relativist personally endorse the approved conduct.
Moral realism need not be directly intuitive because reasoning from ordinary moral intuitions can support realist conclusions.
This states the central intuitionist strategy: begin with accessible first-order judgments and use further reasoning to establish moral realism rather than presupposing it.
Bush's objection that ordinary people lack a sufficiently developed concept of moral realism to possess direct realist intuitions.
Huemer concedes that untrained people may not understand metaethical terminology while maintaining that familiar judgments and consistency principles can ground an argument to realism.
A single plausible context in which a moral claim has genuinely realist content is enough to undermine universal anti-realist accounts of moral language.
The move directly supports realism against contextual and language-use objections by arguing that some ordinary moral discourse asserts truth-apt, attitude-independent content.
Bush's claim that there may be no determinate fact about the metaethical meaning of ordinary moral assertions.
Huemer argues that ethical argument supplies contexts where speakers are neither merely expressing feelings nor reporting attitudes, and where familiar moral premises remain plausible.
Error theory accepts realist semantics and therefore conflicts with common sense by declaring ordinary moral assertions false, not merely by denying stance-independent facts.
This sharpens the principal objection to error theory by locating the conflict in its falsification of ordinary moral claims rather than in an isolated metaphysical denial.
Bush's defense that the error theorist is committed only to denying stance-independent moral facts.
Huemer maintains that error theorists share the realist account of what ordinary assertions purport to report and consequently must reject those assertions as systematically false.
Negative answers to ordinary moral questions bundle normative and metaethical issues, so they can misleadingly imply approval of conduct that error theory does not endorse.
This is Bush's principal answer to the common-sense objection, separating denial of stance-independent facts from first-order opposition to objectionable conduct.
Huemer's argument that error theory straightforwardly denies true ordinary judgments and is therefore radically counterintuitive.
Bush analyzes the ambiguity of denying a moral assertion and argues that an error theorist can vigorously oppose conduct while rejecting the assertion's presumed stance-independent basis.
Even after explicitly canceling any suggestion that an error theorist approves of objectionable conduct, the theory's denial of wrongness remains counterintuitive.
The controlled example directly tests and rejects Bush's proposed explanation of the realist intuition by neutralizing the alleged pragmatic confound.
Bush's claim that error theory seems implausible only because denial of wrongness pragmatically suggests approval of the conduct.
Huemer stipulates an error theorist who strongly condemns the conduct while denying its moral wrongness, then maintains that the resulting position is still deeply implausible.
Training ordinary people enough to understand metaethical questions both removes them from the relevant untrained population and risks biasing the judgments elicited.
The argument challenges the evidential basis of common-sense realism by claiming that the necessary process of making folk judgments measurable contaminates the target phenomenon.
Huemer's suggestion that adequately informed ordinary people could reason from familiar moral judgments toward moral realism.
Bush argues that comprehension requires philosophical education and that such education may itself determine the resulting answer, making claims about an antecedent folk view unreliable.
Ordinary moral assertions can be meaningful without carrying determinate realist or anti-realist commitments because meaning is fixed holistically by communicative use and context.
This presents the anti-realist language-use alternative central to the motion, denying that meaningful ordinary discourse must encode either side's metaethical theory.
Huemer's objection that meaningful ordinary moral claims must have some determinate metaethical content, including realist content in suitable contexts.
Bush separates meaningful communicative purposes from theoretical commitments, treating pragmatic aims as integral to meaning while leaving ordinary speakers metaethically indeterminate.
If the anti-realist explanation rests entirely on pragmatic implications, a context that explicitly neutralizes those implications should leave a distinct and still implausible semantic denial.
The move isolates the disputed semantic content from pragmatic effects and therefore supplies a direct test of Bush's contextual explanation of realist intuitions.
Bush's claim that the apparent implausibility of denying familiar moral statements derives from their pragmatic implications rather than semantic content.
Huemer reformulates Bush's account, then imagines a speaker who strongly opposes the conduct while expressly denying its wrongness in order to neutralize ordinary pragmatic inferences.

Even after pragmatic implications are stipulated away, reactions favoring realism may remain pragmatically influenced, and existing survey evidence cannot establish which interpretation people would favor under genuinely neutral conditions.
This challenges the evidential force of Huemer's linguistic and intuitive plausibility tests by arguing that their supposedly neutral conditions have not been empirically achieved.
Huemer's attempt to neutralize pragmatic implications and preserve the implausibility of denying that torturing babies is wrong.

Huemer had reformulated the torture example to remove ordinary practical implications; Bush responds that residual pragmatic influence and uncertainty about respondents still undermine the proposed inference to realism.
Whether pain is bad cannot be assessed through an undifferentiated intuition because the answer changes with the realist, anti-realist, or stipulatively preference-based meaning assigned to badness.
The move directly contests the intuitionist method by denying that an unanalysed appearance of truth can discriminate stance-independent value from trivial preference-relative truth.
Huemer's proposed axiological analogue in which saying that pain is not bad but merely disliked still appears implausible.

After Huemer asks whether axiological judgments support realism like deontic judgments, Bush argues that the apparent truth of pain's badness depends entirely on what kind of truth and badness are intended.

People can intuit whether a statement is true before specifying its analysis, as illustrated by Gettier-style counterexamples whose ability to refute an analysis would otherwise be rendered circular and useless.
This supplies a general defense of the pre-analytic intuitions required by Huemer's moral methodology and answers the objection that meanings must first be unpacked.
Bush's claim that he cannot judge an unanalysed normative statement without first knowing its realist or anti-realist presuppositions.
Bush had argued that truth intuitions depend on prior semantic interpretation; Huemer counters through the methodological role of stopped-clock and Gettier cases in testing proposed analyses.

Gettier cases do not reveal analytic truths about knowledge because the question merely probes dispositions to use an ambiguous English word, which is not a suitable method for discovering a language-independent essence.
The argument rejects the broader analytic-philosophical methodology on which Huemer's appeal to intuitive counterexamples and process-of-elimination reasoning depends.
Huemer's defense of pre-analytic truth intuitions through the stopped-clock Gettier counterexample to justified-true-belief analysis.
Huemer treated Gettier judgments as proof that intuitions can precede analysis; Bush denies both that such cases disclose analytic facts and that word-use dispositions could discover them.

There need be no determinate phenomenon corresponding to the English word knowledge, and anti-realism remains logically available when one rejects the linguistic, psychological, and metaphilosophical assumptions built into Huemer's restricted possibility space.
The move identifies a foundational disagreement that blocks Huemer's elimination of anti-realism rather than merely disputing a particular moral example or isolated intuition.
Huemer's request for clarification about Bush's denial of truths concerning what knowledge is and the method for identifying them.

Bush expands his methodological objection into quietism about conceptual essences and argues that Huemer's elimination strategy presupposes a contested analytic framework rather than exhausting anti-realist options.

Philosophical intuitions may be context-induced pseudo-phenomenology: students can be trained into an idiosyncratic Anglophone philosophical mode of reporting experiences rather than detecting universal normative or conceptual truths.
This offers a causal debunking explanation for the intuitive appearances on which ethical intuitionism relies, challenging their reliability without needing to refute each intuition individually.
Huemer's appeal to the large majority who report the expected intuitive response to Gettier cases and similar philosophical examples.

Asked why most people give the standard response, Bush contrasts his own lack of determinate reactions and hypothesizes that philosophical instruction prompts reports resembling learned pseudo-phenomenology.

Responses to under-specified truth and knowledge questions may reflect pragmatic completion or spontaneously supplied interpretations, while linguistic evidential systems and cross-cultural variation make the resulting intuitions an unresolved empirical matter.

The move supplies multiple empirically testable alternatives to treating convergent verbal responses as direct access to objective truth, thereby weakening the intuitionist inference at its evidential base.
Huemer's objection that standard intuitions arise even among untrained first-day students and therefore cannot simply be products of philosophical training.

Huemer challenged the training hypothesis with novice agreement; Bush answers that prompts invite implicit interpretation and that language structure, culture, and pragmatics mediate what respondents say.
Cross-cultural conceptual variation may diminish the philosophical importance of parochial thick concepts, but it does not eliminate shared thin normative concepts such as better and worse.
The distinction preserves a cross-culturally relevant target for realism even if particular moral vocabularies or concepts fail to translate exactly across languages and traditions.
Bush's argument that intuitions and knowledge judgments may vary with language, culture, conceptual framing, and evidential grammar.

Huemer concedes that translated concepts may differ and that parochial concepts can be less interesting, while maintaining that thinner evaluative notions remain recognizable across conceptual schemes.

Empirical findings about cultures lacking familiar morality vocabulary deserve philosophical attention even if individual studies are inconclusive, because philosophy should incorporate relevant data while remaining cautious about overextended empirical inferences.

The move supports the anti-realist challenge to armchair universality claims by grounding conceptual diversity in empirical inquiry while explicitly guarding against simplistic scientistic conclusions.
Huemer's discussion of cross-cultural concepts and suggestion that concepts without translation may be philosophically less interesting despite correct local judgments.
Bush cites research on alternative normative terminology, stresses that one paper cannot settle the issue, and advocates greater use of disciplined empirical evidence in philosophical disputes.

Even if morality is a historically constructed category with no sharp moral–nonmoral boundary, that does not decide realism, because the substantive dispute can continue over stance-independent obligations, reasons, and other thin normative facts.
This sharply identifies the debate's true target by preventing linguistic or genealogical claims about morality from substituting for an argument against stance-independent normativity itself.
Huemer's proposal that culturally variable thick moral concepts can be set aside while realism remains focused on thin concepts such as better and worse.

After the discussion of Mongolian and ancient Greek concepts, Bush explains that revisionary accounts of morality are compatible with realism and therefore do not by themselves establish his broader anti-realism.
Moral aversion differs from self-interested or emotional aversion because moral judgment can motivate action even when emotion and preference favor violating an obligation.
The distinction between ethical intuition and ordinary preference directly supports intuitionism against an objection that collapses both into one kind of aversion.
The preceding question argues that aversion to harming a puppy may be indistinguishable from aversion to harming oneself.
Huemer distinguishes self-interest, emotion, and moral judgment, then uses promise-keeping against one's desires as a clearer case of distinct moral phenomenology.
Subjective preferences need not be less important than stance-independent facts, whose alleged authority supplies no motivation beyond an agent's own goals and desires.
This defends anti-realism against the central charge that subjectivity diminishes moral importance, authority, or motivational force.
The audience question suggests that calling morality subjective makes it less important and less authoritative.
Bush argues that evaluative importance is itself stance-dependent, denies that external moral facts inherently motivate or command, and compares morality with sufficient subjective food preferences.
Objective morality is harder to evade than preference-based morality, and moral reasons may outweigh prudential reasons in a way that preference-derived reasons cannot.
The response supplies the realist account of the additional authority that Bush had argued stance-independent facts could not intelligibly possess.
Bush argues that stance-independent facts add no intelligible authority or motivational force beyond subjective preferences.
Huemer says preference-dependent requirements can be dismissed when they conflict with what one wants, whereas objective requirements resist that escape and can override prudential considerations.

Removing unusual metaphysical commitments from non-naturalist realism does not answer the anti-realist's deeper conceptual concern that external reasons and irreducible normativity may be unintelligible.
The move clarifies that Bush's rejection of realism rests on conceptual intelligibility rather than metaphysical queerness, preserving his objection against minimalist realism.
The question proposes conceptual moral truths as a way to retain moral truth while avoiding external moral properties.

Bush distinguishes his position from metaphysical queerness arguments and maintains that stripped-down realist theories still depend on external reasons or irreducible facts that require coherent explanation.

An anti-realist who accepts ordinary moral judgments must explain them through expressivism or attitude reports, alternatives vulnerable respectively to embedding problems and counterexamples involving changed attitudes.
This restates the realist eliminative argument that prominent anti-realist interpretations cannot adequately preserve apparently true first-order moral judgments.
The question describes anti-realists who accept that some moral judgments seem true while denying objective moral properties.
Huemer divides anti-realist explanations into expressive and attitude-reporting approaches, invoking embedding difficulties against the former and altered-attitude scenarios against the latter.

Whether ordinary people hold a determinate realist commitment is an empirical and domain-specific question, so confidence about external-world belief does not justify attributing folk metaethical realism.
The argument protects folk metaethical indeterminacy from an attempted generalization involving external-world and scientific realism.
The question asks whether skepticism about attributing folk moral realism must also apply to external-world and scientific realism.

Bush allows that people probably reject external-world skepticism while noting uncertainty about correspondence theories and insisting that determinacy must be evaluated separately across philosophical domains.

Belief in anti-realism could weaken moral commitment because agents who treat moral reasons as mere preference satisfaction may abandon costly beneficence when self-directed alternatives satisfy them more.
The practical-consequences argument supports realism's claimed normative force, though it concerns psychological effects rather than directly establishing moral facts.
The moderator asks whether subjectivism and related anti-realist views entail or produce harmful consequences.
Huemer predicts reduced moral commitment under subjectivism and illustrates the prediction by contrasting charitable sacrifice with stronger satisfaction of personal preferences.
Neither anti-realism nor realism entails behavioral consequences; their effects are contingent empirical matters, and realism itself could foster dogmatism or rationalize atrocities.
The response directly rebuts the practical case for realism and reverses it by identifying symmetrical psychological risks associated with realist belief.
Huemer argues that accepting anti-realism may weaken moral commitment and reduce costly altruistic behavior.

Bush separates truth from contingent psychological impact, predicts little behavioral change from anti-realism, and argues that realism may instead encourage rigid obedience to purported objective truths.
Philosophers use intuition for multiple phenomena, some ordinary and genuine but others potentially pseudo-psychological states produced by mistaken theories of cognition and phenomenology.
This develops the anti-intuitionist challenge to the epistemic faculty on which Huemer's realist methodology substantially relies.
The question asks what should replace intuition as the name for dispositions to affirm basic propositions.

Bush emphasizes varied philosophical definitions, accepts innocuous belief dispositions, but warns that quasi-perceptual truth-detecting faculties may reflect theoretical misdescription rather than real mental states.

The realism dispute should be relocated to metaphilosophy because moral realism arises from misguided assumptions about knowledge, intuition, language, and meaning, while anti-realism has broader conceptual resources than standard taxonomies suggest.
The closing thesis states Bush's overarching reason for rejecting the standard realist dialectic and integrates his epistemic, linguistic, and quietist objections.

Bush locates the fundamental disagreement in background metaphilosophy, portrays realism as a byproduct of defective presuppositions, aligns his approach with dissident traditions, and reasserts anti-realist conceptual flexibility.
Standard positive arguments for moral realism have straightforward and compelling anti-realist responses and do not provide strong support for realism.
This directly challenges the affirmative case by claiming that convergence and related positive arguments fail to establish moral realism over anti-realism.
Positive arguments offered or available in support of objective moral realism.
After continuing an earlier point about anti-realist conceptual resources, Bush turns to positive realist arguments and claims anti-realists can answer them effectively.
Moral realism has no privileged common-sense or default status, so realists must supply arguments rather than place the burden on anti-realists.
The move contests the dialectical burden of proof and rejects a presumptive advantage that would otherwise favor realism without independent argument.
The realist presumption that moral realism is the common-sense default and anti-realists bear the burden.
Bush concludes his closing statement by denying that realism occupies a privileged starting position and urging anti-realists to demand affirmative realist arguments.
Ethical intuitions are initial intellectual appearances in which a proposition seems true through reflection rather than inference from another belief.
Defining intuition as a noninferential intellectual appearance supplies the central epistemic concept required for Huemer's defense of ethical intuitionism.
Earlier objections and questions concerning what intuitions are and how appeals to them should be understood.
In his closing statement, Huemer distinguishes sensory, memory, inferential, and initial intellectual appearances before identifying intuitions with the final category.
Appearances are the basis of every plausibly justified belief, and rejecting a presumption that things are as they appear would eliminate justification altogether.
The argument provides the general epistemic foundation for treating ethical intuitions as prima facie credible rather than dismissing them as evidentially inert.
Earlier challenges to why ethical intuitions should receive evidential weight or presumptive credibility.
Having defined intuitions as appearances, Huemer argues that rational belief generally depends on what seems true and contrasts this with self-deception and wishful thinking.
Realism itself need not be the default; the relevant presumption favors appearances, from which the way morality appears to most people can support realism.
This directly answers Bush's burden-of-proof objection by relocating the presumption from realism as a doctrine to appearances as general evidence.
Bush's claim that moral realism lacks privileged default status and must be supported without presumption.
Huemer partially accepts that realism is not itself presumptively true but argues that ordinary appearances receive a presumption and can ground arguments to realism.
The principal arguments from queerness, moral disagreement, and evolutionary debunking do not provide good support for anti-realism or moral skepticism.
The move rejects several major routes to anti-realism and concludes that anti-realist commitment is driven more by intuition than by successful argument.
Anti-realist arguments based on moral facts being queer, widespread disagreement, and evolutionary debunking.
Huemer surveys traditional queerness and disagreement arguments plus evolutionary skepticism, summarizes their intended force, and dismisses them as unsuccessful arguments for anti-realism.
